tier_reason: Every claimed number is in the ywasm column of the dmonad/crdt-benchmarks README N=6000 table (i5-8400, Node 20.5.0, harness benchmarks/ywasm/factory.js plus js-lib public), but the suite's author Kevin Jahns is also a listed maintainer and MIT copyright holder of y-crdt (and the author of the Yjs baseline), so for ywasm these are first-party numbers, not an independent suite. Not A because the prebuilt ywasm 0.9.3 npm package's wasm build flags are not stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: dmonad/crdt-benchmarks README, N=6000, i5-8400, Node 20.5.0, ywasm 0.9.3 vs yjs 13.6.11. Update time: ywasm faster on B1.1 append (154 vs 188 ms), B1.3 prepend (23 vs 119 ms, 5.2x, derived from page data), B1.4 random inserts (128 vs 131 ms), B1.7 (141 vs 158 ms), B1.8 append numbers (29 vs 148 ms, 5.1x, derived) and B1.10 prepend numbers (28 vs 122 ms, 4.4x, derived); slower on B1.5 (449 vs 154 ms), B1.11 (144 vs 134 ms), B2.2 (365 vs 65 ms), B2.3 (1,014 vs 85 ms), B2.4 (2,786 vs 178 ms), B3.1-B3.4 (278-299 vs 72-86 ms), B4 real-world trace (28,675 vs 5,714 ms, 5.0x slower) and B4x100 (2,829,633 vs 608,908 ms, 4.6x slower). Load time: ywasm parseTime is lower on 20 of 21 rows (B4 16 vs 39 ms, B4x100 1,328 vs 2,622 ms). Bundle 677,667 vs 69,124 bytes. Overall ywasm loses 11 of the 17 non-trivial update-time rows to Yjs, including the real-world trace; its only consistent win is parse/load time. The y-crdt README itself makes no speed claim.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Node 20.5.0 (node --expose-gc run.js); prebuilt ywasm 0.9.3 npm package, wasm build flags not stated
corrections.workload: dmonad/crdt-benchmarks suite at N=6000 in Node: B1 single-user text/array edits (B1.1-B1.11), B2 two-user concurrent edits, B3 20*sqrt(N) clients writing a map/array, B4 replay of a real-world editing trace and B4x100; time, parseTime, encodeTime, docSize and bundle size per library.
corrections.caveats: Mixed result, not an overall win: ywasm is about 5x slower than Yjs on the real-world trace (B4, B4x100), about 16x slower on concurrent insert/delete (B2.4), 3-12x slower on the other concurrent rows (B2.2, B2.3, B3.1-B3.4), and its bundle is about 10x larger; it wins prepend/append microbenchmarks and parse/load time. The suite is written by Kevin Jahns, author of Yjs and a listed maintainer and copyright holder of y-crdt, so it is not independent of either side. The table is stale: crdt-benchmarks' last commit is 2024-02-12, its results table measured ywasm 0.9.3 while the harness now pins ywasm ^0.17.4 and y-crdt has since released v0.28, so current ywasm may differ in either direction. memUsed shows 0 B for wasm because it excludes wasm memory. ywasm is the wasm/JS binding of the yrs Rust core in the same repo.

notes: Numbers verified row by row in the ywasm column; the record's numbers were right but it omitted most of the losing rows (B1.5, B2.2, B2.3, B3.x) and the parseTime wins, now corrected. Downgraded B to C because the benchmark author co-maintains y-crdt (this differs from the Loro entry, which was kept at B from the same table because Loro is unrelated to the suite author). Shortcomings to record: slower than Yjs on the real-world trace and on all concurrent workloads, stale 0.9.3 table, 10x larger bundle, no wasm build flags. Metadata holds: MIT, 2.2k stars, last commit 2026-09-30, active.

tier_reason: First-party README output (24.63 ms vs tar-js 3,943.50 ms and tarts 1,251.60 ms on a Xeon Platinum 8269CY) from the public harness examples/nodejs-benchmark/bench.ts; Node, rustc and wasm-pack versions are not stated and the >50x gain is capped at C anyway. The large ratio comes mostly from both JS baselines reallocating and copying the whole archive on every appended file (quadratic), not from wasm.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: wasm-pack build --target nodejs (Makefile) with the Cargo release profile opt-level = "s" (Cargo.toml); rustc, wasm-pack, wasm-bindgen and Node versions not stated; benchmark run via ts-node
corrections.workload: Building an uncompressed tar archive in memory from 1,001 generated lorem-ipsum text files (3 paragraphs each) in Node.js (examples/nodejs-benchmark/bench.ts); each library runs once, cold, one after the other in the same process, with no warm-up, repetitions or output comparison.
corrections.caveats: Single cold run of each library on small text files, results from 'my machine' (Xeon Platinum 8269CY), Node and toolchain versions not stated; the README output was printed by an earlier version of bench.ts (labels differ from the current script). Both baselines are quadratic writers: tar-js 0.3.0 (lib/utils.js extend) allocates a buffer just large enough, rounded to 10,240 bytes, zero-fills it with a byte-by-byte JS loop and copies the whole archive, up to twice per appended file; tarts 2.0.1 (tarts.js) builds the archive with reduce, allocating a new Uint8Array of size a+b and copying the whole archive for every file. tar-wasm wraps the Rust tar crate (tar 0.4.38) over a Vec<u8> with amortized growth, so the 50-160x mostly measures the baselines' O(n^2) buffer growth; widely used JS tar writers (tar-stream, node-tar) were not compared. The README asterisk says 'depending on the browser' but only a Node run is shown. Every entry gets mode 0777, uid/gid 0 and mtime 0. set_gzip(true) compresses with yazi Format::Zlib, so the 'gzip' option emits a zlib stream rather than a gzip file (not on the benchmarked path). Repository archived by the owner on 2025-07-21; last commit 2023-01-24.

notes: README numbers and harness match the record; metadata holds (MIT, 106 stars, archived 2025-07-21, last commit 2023-01-24, abandoned). Shortcomings to record: both JS baselines are quadratic buffer-growth writers (tar-js extend per file, tarts reduce concat), so the ratio overstates a wasm advantage; single cold run, no warm-up, no output check; versions not stated; set_gzip emits zlib not gzip; archived.

tier_reason: First-party vitest bench output in the README matches every claimed number, and the harness (src/index.bench.ts) and build flags (build.sh; CI pins the emscripten/emsdk:6.0.12 image) are public, but no CPU model or Node version accompanies the example results and the bench workflow page shows no output, so not A; no independent measurement, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: emcc -std=c89 -O3 -flto -msimd128 -mavx2 -sSTRICT -sPURE_WASI -sNO_ASSERTIONS -sNO_FILESYSTEM -sMALLOC=emmalloc -sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH -DARGON2_NO_THREADS -D__AVX2__ on the unmodified phc-winner-argon2 submodule (build.sh); CI builds with the docker image emscripten/emsdk:6.0.12 (.github/actions/emscripten/action.yml), but the README example results do not say which build or Node version produced them
corrections.caveats: Baselines are other wasm libraries (hash-wasm 4.12.0, itself a listed tier-A entry, and libsodium-wrappers-sumo 0.8.4 per package.json), not native argon2, Node's built-in crypto.argon2 (the README itself points to the native Node.js and Bun implementations) or a JS implementation, so this is a wasm-versus-wasm win that does not meet the category's native or JS baselines. The gain comes from building phc-winner-argon2's opt.c AVX2 path through Emscripten's AVX2-to-SIMD128 emulation (requires wasm SIMD support in the runtime). The hash-wasm side creates a new WASMInterface and grows its memory to memorySize on every argon2id call (lib/argon2.ts), while @phi-ag/argon2 reuses one initialized instance outside the timed loop; that is a real API cost of hash-wasm but inflates the 'fast' (512 KiB, about 3 ms) ratio. Hardware and Node version are not stated; the example output was printed by vitest 3.1.4 while package.json now pins vitest 5.0.3, so the library versions behind the example are uncertain. Single-threaded on both sides (ARGON2_NO_THREADS) even with parallelism 4.

notes: README numbers, harness and build script verified; metadata holds (MIT, 13 stars, last commit 2026-10-11, active, not a fork). Off-baseline (baseline_in_list false is correct): it beats other wasm builds, including the listed hash-wasm, not the native library or JS. Shortcomings to record: wasm-vs-wasm only, native Node crypto.argon2 not compared, per-call instantiation on the hash-wasm side, no hardware or Node version, example output from an older vitest.
